A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to acute-onset slurred speech.  He also has right-sided weakness but denies any trauma, headache, or loss of consciousness.  His medical problems include hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus.  The patient has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years.  Neurologic examination shows right-sided lower facial weakness with sparing of the forehead muscles.  Motor strength is 3/5 on the right and 5/5 on the left with a Babinski response on the right.  There is also dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia involving his right upper and lower extremities.  MRI of the brain reveals an acute lacunar infarct in the left basis pontis at the level of the middle cerebellar peduncle, as shown in the image below.

Which of the following cranial nerves exits the brainstem closest to the level affected by this patient's stroke?​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​
explanation:
This patient has an acute lacunar ischemic stroke affecting the left ventral mid-pons (basis pontis) at the level of the middle cerebellar peduncle. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) exits the brainstem from the lateral mid-pons at this same rostrocaudal level, making it the cranial nerve that exits closest to the site of infarction.

Infarcts involving the ventral pons can affect the corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiparesis, Babinski sign) and corticobulbar tract (contralateral lower facial weakness with forehead sparing, dysarthria).  Involvement of corticopontine fibers can also produce ataxic hemiparesis with contralateral dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia.  Unlike true cerebellar lesions, which typically cause ipsilateral coordination deficits, ventral pontine lesions cause contralateral cerebellar findings because affected pontocerebellar fibers decussate before entering the cerebellum through the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle.

(Choice A)  The facial nucleus is located in the caudal pons, and the facial nerve exits at the ventrolateral pontomedullary junction, which is inferior to the level of this infarct.  This patient's forehead sparing indicates that his facial weakness is due to a corticobulbar tract lesion rather than direct involvement of the facial nucleus or facial nerve.

(Choice B)  The hypoglossal nucleus is located medially on the floor of the fourth ventricle at the level of the medulla, and the nerve exits at the rostral end of the preolivary sulcus.

(Choice C)  The oculomotor nucleus is located in the rostral midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus and red nucleus, and the nerve exits at the interpeduncular fossa.

(Choice E)  The trochlear nucleus is located in the caudal midbrain, and the nerve exits the dorsal midbrain just below the inferior colliculus (below the red nucleus).  The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to decussate before innervating its target (superior oblique muscle).

Educational objective:Infarcts involving the ventral mid-pons can produce dysarthria and contralateral hemiparesis/lower facial palsy due to disruption of the ipsilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.  The trigeminal nerve arises from the lateral mid-pons at the level of the middle cerebellar peduncle.​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​
